steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper proposing WAS, a framework that both selects and weighs multiple graph pre-training tasks per instance. Motivate it from the limits of single tasks and weighing-only methods, present our preliminary investigation of task importance and compatibility, and finish with the framework and our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Graphs, GNNs, and graph pre-training
- Weighing multiple tasks: prior work and its limits
- Investigation: importance vs. compatibility
- Research question: selecting and weighing
- WAS framework and contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Background
  - real-world relationships (social media, molecules, transportation) -> graphs
  - GNNs (cite): powerful for relation-dependent tasks
  - mostly supervised/semi-supervised; labels expensive and limited
  - graph pre-training (cite): fewer annotated labels, massive unlabeled data; extract knowledge, transfer to downstream tasks
  - hundreds of pre-training tasks (cite); Fig. 1(a): no single task best on all datasets
- Weighing multiple tasks
  - integrating / linearly weighing tasks more effective than more complex tasks
  - AutoSSL (cite): task-loss weights from pseudo-homophily measure
  - ParetoGNN (cite): dynamic weights promoting Pareto optimality
  - AUX-TS (cite): adaptive combination, but in fine-tuning stage
  - all three global; ignore instance specificities (nodes in social network, graphs in molecular dataset)
  - AGSSL (cite): instance-level weighing in fine-tuning
  - all focus on importance, ignore compatibility (conflicts between tasks) -> weighing alone can't fix
  - larger task pool -> compatibility worse, no further performance growth -> need selection
  - prior works only node-level evaluation, not graph-level; Table. 1 compares with WAS
- Investigation (Fig. 1(c))
  - tasks: AttrMask (AM), ContextPred (CP) (cite), EdgePred (EP) (cite), GPT-GNN (cite), GraphCL (cite), GraphLoG (cite), InfoGraph (IG) (cite)
  - conclusion: importance weighing and task selecting both important; importance vs. compatibility
  - Fig. 1(b): AM + CP under varying \lambda; best at \lambda\!=\!0.4
  - weighing ignores compatibility -> limits performance
  - Fig. 1(c): not all combinations help; AM + GraphCL -7.08 drop -> need suitable combinations
  - only pairs shown; bigger pool -> more complex combinations, more severe conflicts
- Research question
  - how to address importance and compatibility when integrating tasks in fine-tuning?
  - (1) task selecting: optimal combination from task pool by compatibility
  - (2) importance weighing: weigh selected tasks
  - related/collaborative; important tasks selected more, but importance-only selection -> conflicts
  - AutoSSL, ParetoGNN, AUX-TS, AGSSL: weighing only, overlook selecting
- WAS and contributions
  - Weigh And Select (WAS); decoupled siamese networks
  - (1) per-instance task combination sampled from distribution based on compatibility; (2) weights for selected tasks by importance
  - first weighing & selecting strategy for graph pre-training tasks
  - 16 datasets; comparable to leading counterparts, node-level and graph-level
  - contributions: (1) limits of weighing-only, importance of selecting; (2) first to identify select and weigh; experiments on why collaboration matters, difference from weighing-only, why decouple; (3) framework: adaptive, dynamic, compatible selecting and weighing per instance

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Relationships between entities in many real-world applications, like social media, molecules, and transportation, can be modeled naturally as graphs. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown powerful capabilities for handling relation-dependent tasks. But most existing work on GNNs is in supervised or semi-supervised settings, which need labeled data and so are expensive and limited. Recent advances in graph pre-training aim to reduce the need for annotated labels and make it possible to train on massive unlabeled data. The main purpose of graph pre-training is to extract informative knowledge from massive unlabeled data, and then this learned knowledge can be transferred to specific downstream tasks. Hundreds of graph pre-training tasks have been proposed for this, but as Fig. 1(a) shows, no single pre-training task performs best for all datasets.

So integrating multiple tasks, or more specifically weighing them linearly, has become a more effective approach than designing more complex tasks. For example, AutoSSL combines the weights of task losses based on a pseudo-homophily measure, and ParetoGNN reconciles pre-training tasks by assigning weights dynamically to promote Pareto optimality. Another related work is AUX-TS, which also combines different tasks adaptively, but it does this combination in the fine-tuning stage. But all three works weigh tasks globally, and they ignore that different instances (e.g., nodes in a social network or graphs in a molecular dataset) can have their own specificities. To solve this, AGSSL was proposed, which learns instance-level task weighing strategies during the fine-tuning stage. Still, these works weigh all tasks and only focus on the importance issue, and they ignore the compatibility issue, i.e., the possible conflicts between different tasks, which simply weighing all tasks cannot resolve. Even worse, the compatibility issue gets more severe as the task pool expands, so existing methods lose the ability to keep gaining performance. So it is necessary to select some tasks to solve this. Also, previous works only evaluated their effectiveness on node-level tasks and neglected graph-level tasks. We summarize the properties of these methods in Table. 1 and compare them with WAS.

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Relationships between entities in many real-world applications, like social media, molecules, and transportation, can be modeled naturally as graphs. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have shown powerful capabilities for handling relation-dependent tasks. But most existing work on GNNs is in supervised or semi-supervised settings, which need labeled data and so are expensive and limited. Recent advances in graph pre-training aim to reduce the need for annotated labels and make it possible to train on massive unlabeled data. The main purpose of graph pre-training is to extract informative knowledge from massive unlabeled data, and then this learned knowledge can be transferred to specific downstream tasks. Hundreds of graph pre-training tasks have been proposed for this, but as Fig. 1(a) shows, no single pre-training task performs best for all datasets.

So integrating multiple tasks, or more specifically weighing them linearly, has become a more effective approach than designing more complex tasks. For example, AutoSSL combines the weights of task losses based on a pseudo-homophily measure, and ParetoGNN reconciles pre-training tasks by assigning weights dynamically to promote Pareto optimality. Another related work is AUX-TS, which also combines different tasks adaptively, but it does this combination in the fine-tuning stage. But all three works weigh tasks globally, and they ignore that different instances (e.g., nodes in a social network or graphs in a molecular dataset) can have their own specificities. To solve this, AGSSL was proposed, which learns instance-level task weighing strategies during the fine-tuning stage. Still, these works weigh all tasks and only focus on the importance issue, and they ignore the compatibility issue, i.e., the possible conflicts between different tasks, which simply weighing all tasks cannot resolve. Even worse, the compatibility issue gets more severe as the task pool expands, so existing methods lose the ability to keep gaining performance. So it is necessary to select some tasks to solve this. Also, previous works only evaluated their effectiveness on node-level tasks and neglected graph-level tasks. We summarize the properties of these methods in Table. 1 and compare them with WAS.

We want to raise several issues by investigating several classical graph pre-training tasks, including AttrMask (AM), ContextPred (CP), EdgePred (EP), GPT-GNN, GraphCL, GraphLoG, and InfoGraph (IG), as shown in Fig. 1(c). First we draw an interesting conclusion: both importance weighing and task selecting are quite important, the first addresses task importance and the second addresses task compatibility.

Fig. 1(b) compares the performance for varying importance weights \lambda when AM and CP are combined. The best performance is achieved at \lambda\!=\!0.4. Task weighing focuses on the importance of each task, but it neglects the compatibility between different tasks, and this limits existing methods from getting higher performance. The results in Fig. 1(c) show how big the impact of the compatibility issue is when multiple tasks are integrated. Not all combinations bring performance improvements, and some even degrade performance (the combination of AM and GraphCL brings a -7.08 drop), which shows that selecting suitable task combinations is necessary. Note that Fig. 1(c) only shows combinations of two tasks. As the task pool expands, the combinations get more complex, and conflicts between different tasks may get more severe.

Based on these investigations, we ask: How can we address the importance and compatibility issues between different tasks when we integrate them during the fine-tuning stage? We identify two key issues in the combining process: (1) task selecting – how to select an optimal combination from a given task pool based on task compatibility, (2) importance weighing – how to weigh the importance of the selected tasks. These two are clearly related or collaborative. More important tasks should be selected more, but selecting tasks only based on importance can lead to severe task conflicts. Previous works, AutoSSL, ParetoGNN, AUX-TS, and AGSSL, have focused on importance weighing, but they all overlooked task selecting, and so they cannot keep gaining performance as the task pool grows larger.

In this paper we propose a new framework, Weigh And Select (WAS), for task selecting and importance weighing. The two collaborative processes are combined in decoupled siamese networks, where (1) an optimal combination of tasks is selected for each instance using a sampling distribution calculated from task compatibility, and (2) then task weights are calculated for the selected tasks according to their importance. As far as we know, this work is the first attempt to use a weighing & selecting strategy to integrate multiple graph pre-training tasks. Extensive experiments on 16 datasets show that WAS can achieve comparable performance to other leading counterparts for both node-level and graph-level tasks. Our contributions are: (1) We show the limitations of current weighing-only schemes and show the importance of the task selecting process. (2) As far as we know, we are the first to identify two important collaborative processes, select and weigh; we provide extensive experiments to explain in detail why their collaboration is important, how it is different from weighing-only methods and why the two processes need to be decoupled. (3) We propose a new framework that selects and weighs multiple pre-training tasks adaptively, dynamically, and compatibly for each instance separately.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Relationships between entities in various real-world applications, such as social media, molecules, and transportation, can be naturally modeled as graphs. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) [1,2,3,4,5] have demonstrated their powerful capabilities to handle relation-dependent tasks. However, most of the existing work in GNNs is focused on supervised or semi-supervised settings, which require labeled data and hence are expensive and limited. Recent advances in graph pre-training [6,7,8] aim to reduce the need for annotated labels and enable training on massive unlabeled data. The primary purpose of graph pre-training is to extract informative knowledge from massive unlabeled data and the learned knowledge can then be transferred to some specific downstream tasks. While hundreds of graph pre-training tasks have been proposed in this regard [9,10,11,12,13,14], as shown in Fig. 1(a), there is no single pre-training task that performs best for all datasets.

Therefore, integrating multiple tasks, or more specifically weighing them linearly, has emerged as a more effective approach than designing more complex tasks. For example, AutoSSL [15] combines the weights of task losses based on a pseudo-homophily measure, and ParetoGNN [16] reconciles pre-training tasks by dynamically assigning weights that promote the Pareto optimality. Another related work is AUX-TS [17], which also combines different tasks adaptively, but this combination happens in the fine-tuning stage. However, all three works perform task weighing in a global manner, ignoring the fact that different instances (e.g., nodes in a social network or graphs in a molecular dataset) may have their own specificities. To solve this, AGSSL [18] has been proposed to learn instance-level task weighing strategies during the fine-tuning stage. Nonetheless, these works to weigh all tasks focus only on the importance issue, but ignore the compatibility issue, i.e., the possible conflicts between different tasks, which cannot be resolved by simply weighing all tasks. Even worse, as the task pool expands, compatibility issue becomes more severe, which deprives existing methods of the ability to keep gaining performance growth. Therefore, it is necessary to select some tasks to solve it. In addition, previous works have only evaluated their effectiveness on node-level tasks but neglected graph-level tasks. We have summarized the properties of these methods in Table. 1 and compared them with WAS.

We would like to raise several issues through investigation on several classical graph pre-training tasks, including AttrMask (AM), ContextPred (CP) [10], EdgePred (EP) [1], GPT-GNN [19], GraphCL [12], GraphLoG [20], and InfoGraph (IG) [9], as shown in Fig. 1(c). First we draw an interesting conclusion: both importance weighing and task selecting of tasks are quite important, where the former addresses the issue of task importance, while the latter addresses the issue of task compatibility.

Fig. 1(b) compares the performance under varying importance weights \lambda when combining AM and CP. The best performance is achieved at \lambda\!=\!0.4. While task weighing focuses on the importance of each task, it neglects compatibility between different tasks, which limits existing methods from achieving higher performance. The results in Fig. 1(c) show the big impact of the compatibility issue when integrating multiple tasks. It can be seen that not all combinations can bring performance improvements, and some of them even degrade performance (combination of AM and GraphCL brings a -7.08 drop), which highlights the necessity of selecting suitable task combinations. Note that Fig. 1(c) shows only the combination between two tasks. As the task pool expands, such combinations become more complex, and conflicts between different tasks may become more severe.

Based on the above investigations, here we would like to ask: How to address the importance and compatibility issues between different tasks when integrating them during the fine-tuning stage? We identified two key issues in the combining process: (1) task selecting – how to select an optimal combination from a given task pool based on the task compatibility, (2) importance weighing – how to weigh the importance of the selected tasks. These two are clearly related or collaborative. More important tasks should be selected more, but selecting tasks based solely on importance can lead to severe task conflicts. While previous works, AutoSSL, ParetoGNN, AUX-TS, and AGSSL, have focused on importance weighing, they have all overlooked task selecting, which has deprived them of the ability to keep gaining performance growth as the task pool grows larger.

In this paper, we propose a novel framework, Weigh And Select (WAS) for task selecting and importance weighing. The two collaborative processes are combined in decoupled siamese networks, where (1) an optimal combination of tasks is selected for each instance based on a sampling distribution calculated based on the task compatibility, and (2) task weights are then calculated for the selected tasks according to their importance. To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first attempt to use the weighing & selecting strategy for integrating multiple graph pre-training tasks. Experiments on 16 datasets show that WAS can achieve comparable performance to other leading counterparts for both node-level and graph-level tasks. Our contributions are summarized as follows: (1) We show the limitations of current weighing-only schemes and demonstrate the importance of task selecting process. (2) To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to identify two important collaborative processes: select and weigh; we provide extensive experiments to explain in detail why the collaboration of the two is important, how it differs from weighing-only methods and why the two processes need to be decoupled. (3) We propose a novel framework to adaptively, dynamically, and compatibly select and weigh multiple pre-training tasks for each instance separately.
